titre: England's First Women Jurors: The 1919 Act, Then the Filters
accroche: In 1919, a British law forbids excusing a woman from jury service because of her sex. In 1921, Bristol summons 80 women and 333 men.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 23, 1919, the Parliament of the United Kingdom passes the Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act. Its first section forbids disqualifying a person from public office, judicial office, or a civil profession because of sex or marriage, and provides that a person can no longer be exempted from jury service on those same grounds. The Act's schedule repeals the definitions of a juror written into the jury laws of 1870 and 1871.

On July 29, 1920, before the Bristol Quarter Sessions, a jury of six women and six men tries a first case: a theft, in which the defendant is found guilty. A regional history post from the University of the West of England sees in this the first criminal trials before a mixed jury in Great Britain. Two of the women jurors, Mrs. Wellings and Mrs. Yandell, are excused after the first day.

## An open door, with filters on top

The law itself provides safety valves. The judge, the chairman of the quarter sessions, or the recorder may order a jury of men only or of women only, on request or on his own initiative. A woman may also be excused from a case because of the nature of the evidence or of the questions to be decided.

The heaviest filter is a quieter one: the property qualification, inherited from the Juries Act of 1825. To serve as a juror, one had to meet property conditions. In Bristol, only 43% of the women summoned to the quarter sessions are heads of household, which, according to the author of a study of the registers, should have made them ineligible under those rules; city officials grumbled about these conditions for a time. Elsewhere, the admission of women recedes: at the end of 1920, in ten large cities that had never required property ownership in order to sit (Juries (Emergency) Act 1920).

The jury registers of Bristol give an order of magnitude. In 1921, the city summons 80 women and 333 men: fewer than one person in five. In several English cities, women entered on the jury lists make up only about 5% of the female population. In the Law and History Review, Kevin Crosby sums up these years by saying that the 1919 Act widened the right to serve for “some women,” and that restrictions followed almost immediately.

## What this shifts

It is often said that 1919 is the date when women enter the jury. The text says something else: it removes an exclusion based on sex, and leaves intact the system that chooses who sits. Activists argued that the property qualification kept married women off juries until it was abolished in the 1970s. The author of the study of the Bristol registers finds the argument true in broad terms, but less clear-cut at the quarter sessions, where the women summoned are on average four to nine years older than the men.

What actually brought a woman into the jury box was therefore decided elsewhere: in the exemptions granted, in the separate juries a judge could order, in the way each city drew up its list. We would need to know, city by city, the share of women on those lists to know what the 1919 Act produced.

carte.idee: The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act of 1919 forbids excusing a woman from jury service because of her sex. But single-sex juries, exemptions, and the property qualification remained: in Bristol in 1921, the city summons 80 women for 333 men.

quiz.question: What did the 1919 British law leave in place after removing the exclusion of women from the jury?
choix: The property qualification and the power to order a single-sex jury
The requirement to be married and to have one's husband's consent to serve
The reservation of the most serious criminal cases to men only
A quota limiting women to two per jury
quiz.explication: The law left in place the property qualification inherited from 1825 and allowed the judge to order a jury of men only or of women only. It required neither marriage nor the husband's consent and did not reserve criminal cases to men: Bristol tries a theft before a mixed jury as early as July 1920. No quota appears in it.
